turns.content: Hey, I've been dealing with some work stress lately and could use some advice on managing it better.

I'm happy to help you work through this. Work stress is really common, and there are lots of strategies that can make a difference. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been causing the stress? Is it workload, deadlines, relationships with colleagues, or something else?
It's mainly the workload. My company did layoffs a few months ago and now I'm doing the job of like 2.5 people. The expectations haven't changed though.

That's a really difficult situation, and unfortunately very common after layoffs. Being expected to absorb significantly more work without adjusted expectations is genuinely unsustainable. A few thoughts: Have you had a conversation with your manager about prioritization? Sometimes they don't fully realize the cumulative impact. Also, are there any tasks you could push back on or delegate?
I've tried talking to my manager but she's in the same boat. Everyone is stretched thin. She just says to do my best but the deadlines keep coming.

That's frustrating when even your manager doesn't have the power to change things. In situations like this, protecting your own wellbeing becomes essential since you can't pour from an empty cup. Are you able to set any boundaries around work hours? And outside of work, do you have activities or people that help you decompress?
I've been trying to keep work to work hours but it's hard. I used to play basketball with friends on weekends but I've been too tired lately. Most weekends I just catch up on sleep.

It makes sense that you're exhausted - carrying that much extra load takes a real toll. Sleep is important, but I'd gently encourage you not to completely give up the basketball if you can help it. Social activities and exercise are often the first things we drop when stressed, but they're actually what help us cope. Even showing up once a month might help. How long has this been going on?
The layoffs were about 4 months ago. So it's been building since then. I keep thinking it'll get better but it doesn't seem to be improving.

Four months is a significant amount of time to be running on fumes. If the situation at work isn't improving and there's no sign of relief coming, it might be worth considering your longer-term options too - whether that's having a more serious conversation about hiring, looking at what else is out there, or finding ways to make the current situation more sustainable. What does your gut tell you about whether things will change?
Honestly? I don't think they will. The company is struggling financially which is why they did the layoffs. I don't see them hiring anytime soon. But the job market is rough right now too.

You're caught between a rock and a hard place - a draining current job and an uncertain market. That's a legitimately tough position. While you figure out the bigger picture, let's focus on what's within your control. Small things like protecting your lunch break, taking short walks, or even just stepping outside for a few minutes can help. How are you sleeping, aside from the weekend catch-up?
Not great honestly. I wake up in the middle of the night thinking about work stuff. Then I can't fall back asleep because my mind starts racing about everything I need to do.

That sleep disruption is a real red flag for burnout. When work starts invading your sleep, it affects everything - your mood, your energy, your ability to cope with stress. Have you tried any sleep hygiene techniques, like keeping work devices out of the bedroom or having a wind-down routine? Sometimes writing a quick to-do list before bed can help quiet those racing thoughts.

I've tried some of that. The list thing helps a little but then I just lie there feeling like the list is endless. It's weird, I used to be really good at my job and now I just feel like I'm constantly failing.

What you're describing - that shift from feeling competent to feeling like you're constantly failing - is such a painful part of burnout. It's important to recognize that this isn't about your abilities changing. You were good at your job, and you still have those skills. The circumstances have changed in an impossible way. It's like being a great swimmer but someone tripled the length of the pool and kept the same time limit. Are you being hard on yourself about this?
Probably. I know logically it's not my fault but it doesn't feel that way. My performance review is coming up and I'm dreading it. I used to look forward to those.

The gap between what we know logically and what we feel emotionally can be really wide. It's completely understandable to dread the review given the circumstances. Maybe it could help to prepare some talking points about the increased workload and what you've managed to accomplish despite it? Framing it proactively might help you feel more in control of the narrative. How are things outside of work - any support system you can lean on?
My friends are busy with their own stuff. I had a girlfriend but we broke up about two months ago. She said I was never present anymore, always distracted by work. She wasn't wrong.

I'm sorry to hear about the breakup. Losing a relationship while already dealing with work stress is a lot to carry. And there's often this painful irony where the stress makes us withdraw from the people who could support us, which then creates more stress. It sounds like you're going through a particularly hard season right now. Are you staying connected with anyone - family, old friends, anyone?

My family is across the country. We text sometimes but they don't really get what I'm going through. My friends from basketball have kind of stopped inviting me since I kept saying no. I get it, I would too.

It's understandable that you pulled back when you were exhausted, but I'm a little concerned about how isolated things have become. Those friends might welcome you back more than you think - people often understand more than we give them credit for. Would you consider reaching out to one of them, even just to grab a coffee? Sometimes taking that first step is the hardest part, but human connection can be really restorative.
Maybe. It feels like a lot of effort for something that probably won't help. I don't even know what I'd say. 'Hey sorry I disappeared, my life is kind of falling apart'?

You know, that's actually more honest and relatable than you might think. Most people have gone through hard times and would understand. But I hear that it feels like a lot of effort right now. When we're depleted, even small things can feel overwhelming. Can I ask - when you say your life is 'falling apart,' how are you doing emotionally with everything? It sounds like a lot has accumulated.
I don't know. Some days are okay. Other days I just feel this heaviness, like what's the point of any of it. I go to work, come home exhausted, sleep badly, repeat. It's just a cycle.

That heaviness you're describing and the sense of 'what's the point' - I want to take that seriously. When life becomes just an exhausting cycle without joy or meaning, it wears on us in deep ways. Those feelings are a signal that something needs to change, and they deserve attention. Have you thought about talking to someone, like a therapist or counselor? Sometimes having a dedicated space to process everything can really help.
I've thought about it but I don't really have the time or energy to find one. And my insurance isn't great. It's just another thing on the endless list.

I understand - when you're already overwhelmed, adding another task feels impossible, even if it's something that could help. Some people find that their employer has an EAP (Employee Assistance Program) that offers free short-term counseling, and they handle the matching for you. It might be worth a quick check. But regardless of that, I'm glad you're talking about this. How long have you been feeling this heaviness?

Honestly it's been building for a while. Maybe a couple months. Some weeks are worse than others. This week has been bad. I called in sick yesterday even though I wasn't physically sick, I just couldn't face it.

Taking that day sounds like your mind and body were telling you that you needed a break. That's not weakness - that's self-preservation. I'm glad you listened to that. I am a bit concerned though about how things have been building. When you say this week has been bad, can you tell me more about what that looks like for you?
Just really low energy. Not wanting to do anything. I've been skipping meals because I'm not hungry and eating feels pointless. I know that sounds dramatic.

It doesn't sound dramatic at all - it sounds like you're really struggling. Loss of appetite, low energy, withdrawing from things, feelings of pointlessness - these are signs that you're carrying more than anyone should carry alone. I care about how you're doing. When you say things feel pointless, do those thoughts ever go to darker places?
I don't know. Sometimes I just think it would be easier to not exist. Not like I'd do anything, I just get tired of being tired. Of waking up and doing it all again.

Thank you for trusting me with that. What you're describing - wishing you didn't exist, being exhausted by the thought of continuing - those feelings are serious and they matter. I want you to know that this level of pain isn't something you have to just push through alone. You deserve support right now. Would you be willing to reach out to a crisis line like 988, or talk to a doctor soon? This isn't about being dramatic - it's about getting you real help for real pain.
I don't think I'm at crisis level. I'm not going to do anything. I just sometimes wonder if anyone would even notice if I wasn't around. Like would it matter.

I hear you saying you're not going to do anything, and I believe you. But I also want you to know that wondering whether anyone would notice or whether you matter - those thoughts are telling me you're in a lot of pain and feeling very alone. You do matter. Your absence would be felt. I'm concerned about you, and I really think talking to a professional - even just once - could help. You mentioned your ex said you weren't present. Your basketball friends. These are people who valued your presence. Can we talk about one concrete step you could take this week to get some support?
I guess I could look into that EAP thing you mentioned. I just don't want to make a big deal out of nothing.

I'm really glad you're open to that. And I want to gently push back on 'nothing' - months of building stress, sleep problems, a breakup, isolation, skipping meals, thoughts about not existing - that's not nothing. That's a person who's been struggling and deserves help. Looking into the EAP is a real step. Would it help if we talked through how to find that information so it feels less overwhelming? And please, if those darker thoughts get stronger or feel more urgent, 988 is always available. You don't have to be in crisis to call.
